A.explanation: Graph 1 starts at zero and rises, but acceleration of a dropped object starts at a maximum near $g$ and falls. Graph 3 and resultant force do share a shape, but graph 1 cannot be acceleration.

B.explanation: Graph 1 cannot be acceleration against time because it starts at zero. Graph 4 is constant and non-zero, but resultant force must fall to zero at terminal velocity.

C.explanation: Graph 3 starts high and decays to zero, matching acceleration falling to zero, and graph 1 starts at zero and levels to a constant, matching velocity rising to terminal velocity.

D.explanation: Graph 3 can be acceleration, but graph 2 is a straight line through the origin with constant gradient, which means constant acceleration with no air resistance, not velocity approaching terminal velocity.

hints: Notice the starting values: graph 1 starts at $0$ and rises to a plateau, while graph 3 starts at a maximum and decays toward zero.
For a fall from rest with increasing air resistance, connect velocity rising toward terminal velocity with acceleration starting large and falling to zero.
Recall $F = ma$, so resultant force against time must have the same decaying-to-zero shape as acceleration against time, not the rising-to-plateau shape.
walkthrough: The object is dropped from rest, so at $t = 0$ velocity $v = 0$. Weight $mg$ acts down and drag acts up and increases with speed.

Velocity must therefore increase from zero with a decreasing gradient and level off at terminal velocity when drag equals weight. That rising curve with decreasing slope levelling to horizontal is graph 1.

Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph, $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$. It starts at its maximum value and decreases to zero when terminal velocity is reached. That decaying curve from a maximum to zero is graph 3.
Resultant force is $F = ma$ with constant $m$, so its time dependence has exactly the same shape as acceleration, decaying to zero, not the shape of graph 1 or the constant graph 4.
Graph 2 is a straight line from the origin, meaning constant gradient and constant acceleration with no drag effect, so it cannot be the velocity for this resistive fall.
Hence graph 3 fits acceleration and graph 1 fits velocity. This is option C.
